It was formerly played mainly by professional musicians for chiefs, praising their patrons with epics and historical songs. In Burundi it was traditionally played at night for the mwami, was also played to cattle, and is held to be the earliest instrument invented in the country; in Rwanda it is regarded as an important and highly respected instrument. Playing is mostly by men, and children usually teach themselves.

The enanga (inānga) is a traditional plucked instrument of East Africa, found in Burundi, Rwanda, Uganda and parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo; it belongs to the harps and lyres class of chordophones, Hornbostel–Sachs 322.11. It is built around a slightly concave soundboard with a thick frame notched to hold the strings, usually six to eight. The player sits with the instrument on the lap, plucks the full length of the strings and changes the timbre by plucking at different points; it is almost always used to accompany a whisper-like voice singing repeated melodic motifs. It was formerly played mostly by professional musicians for chiefs, and in Burundi it was traditionally played at night while the chief rested, and played for cattle.
演奏者採坐姿，將恩南加豎琴置於腿上，琴身略傾。調音時依五聲音階需要，透過木栓擰緊: The player sits with the enanga on the lap, the body tilted slightly. To tune, the long string running through the notch is tightened or loosened on its wooden peg as the pentatonic scale requires. The sound is made by plucking with the fingers, usually along the full length of the string, though plucking at different points changes the timbre. A beginner can start with holding the instrument, tuning and plucking, then add repeated melodic motifs and sing traditional stories, historical events or everyday matters in a whisper-like voice. Children mostly learn by watching, and the source mentions no systematic tutor.
